design_detail: Narrative review (NEJM Review Article) of the adverse health effects of recreational marijuana use, by four authors at the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, read as the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (published version: N Engl J Med 2014;370(23):2219–2227). No search strategy, inclusion criteria, appraisal of individual studies or pooling; 77 references. Sections: risk of addiction; brain development; possible role as a gateway drug; mental illness; school performance and lifetime achievement; motor-vehicle accidents; cancer and other effects on health; limitations of the evidence and gaps in knowledge (confounding, prenatal exposure, potency, medical uses in a box, policy research); conclusions. Table 1 lists adverse effects of short-term and of long-term or heavy use; Table 2 gives an overall level of confidence (high, medium or low) for nine effects with no stated grading method. Figure 1 (THC in seized samples 1995–2012; emergency department visits 2004–2011) and Figure 2 (perceived risk and daily use among grade-12 students 1975–2013) are images; only their legends were read.
can_establish: What four NIDA authors judged in 2014 to be the best-supported adverse health effects of recreational marijuana use, how confident they said they were in each (Table 2), and which sources they cite for each figure; it can be cited for those judgments, labelled as the authors', and as a pointer to the primary studies.
cannot_establish: That any listed effect is caused by marijuana (the authors say that multiple, often hidden, confounders limit the ability to establish causality for most long-term effects), the size of any risk (every figure is second-hand and several are attributed to reviews or to a source that does not contain them), or the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search); its confidence ratings rest on no stated method.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence was chosen by the authors, who say they focused on the areas where the evidence is strongest (Introduction (unheaded), 2nd paragraph); no databases, dates or criteria are given.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The cited data are mostly from the USA (National Survey on Drug Use and Health 2012–2013, Monitoring the Future 2013, Drug Abuse Warning Network 2004–2011, potency monitoring of seized samples, NESARC through Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011), with cohort, case–control and imaging studies from New Zealand, Australia, Europe and the USA.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. The review covers harms by design and confines medical uses to a box. None of the 77 references has one of the review's authors in its printed author list (editors' count). Several figures come from secondary sources rather than from the primary studies behind them: the adolescent-onset and daily-use dependence figures from the Hall & Degenhardt (2009) narrative review (ref 4; card sc_hall_2009), the doubled crash risk from a source titled "Cannabis effects on driving skills" (ref 37), and imaging, cognitive and educational findings from sources whose titles describe them as reviews (refs 14, 28, 29, 30).

exposure.measurement: Not defined at review level. The review speaks of regular, frequent, heavy, long-term and daily use and of use beginning in adolescence without definitions; the footnote to Table 2 says the ratings concern above all heavy or long-term use and use beginning in adolescence. Dependence figures are DSM-IV dependence where stated (the 9% and the NSDUH counts). Driving statements rest on recent use and blood THC as cited (substantial impairment at 2–5 ng/mL; culpability by THC detection, typical detection minimum 1 ng/mL).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not quantified. Inhalation (smoking) is named as the most common route, with oral use also mentioned (Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph). Lung-cancer exposure is expressed in joint-years (one joint a day for one year), with 30 or more joint-years in the cited case–control study. THC content of seized samples is said to have risen from about 3% in the 1980s to 12% in 2012 (ref 50).
exposure.polysubstance: Named in general terms as a confounder (frequent use with other drugs; tobacco in the cancer studies, where smoking marijuana mixed with tobacco varies by country; alcohol combined with marijuana in driving) but not handled study by study (LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE, 1st paragraph; ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF CANCER AND OTHER EFFECTS ON HEALTH, 1st paragraph; ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF MOTOR-VEHICLE ACCIDENTS, 1st paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not stated for the cognitive and imaging studies cited. The review says cognitive functions are impaired during intoxication and for days afterwards (ref 28) and that cortical CB1 receptor down-regulation reversed after 4 weeks of abstinence (ref 15).

comparison.controls: Varies and is rarely stated: unexposed controls in imaging studies, people who began use as adults (dependence by age of onset), drivers who had used neither drugs nor alcohol (culpability), people who do not smoke (bronchitis symptoms), the general population (life satisfaction).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review says that factors predisposing to both marijuana use and mental illness, and multiple, often hidden, confounders including other drug use, make causal attribution difficult (ADVERSE EFFECTS › RELATION TO MENTAL ILLNESS, 2nd paragraph; LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE, 1st paragraph). Pre-use measurements are not discussed for the imaging studies; the IQ claim rests on one cohort with childhood testing (Meier et al., 2012).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed for the cited studies.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: DSM-IV dependence (NESARC, NSDUH) and withdrawal criteria; diffusion and functional MRI connectivity, regional activity and hippocampal volume; PET CB1 receptor binding; IQ (Dunedin cohort); grades and school dropout; income, need for assistance, unemployment, criminal behaviour and life satisfaction; driving-simulator performance, crash involvement and crash culpability; lung and upper aerodigestive cancers; chronic bronchitis symptoms, airway measures and lung function; myocardial infarction, stroke and transient ischaemic attack; emergency department visits (DAWN).
outcomes.operationalization: Associations are presented as adverse effects: Table 1 is headed as adverse effects of short-term and of long-term or heavy use, and Table 2 rates the level of confidence in the evidence for adverse effects, while its footnote says the ratings concern the association between marijuana use and each effect. Addiction means DSM-IV dependence. Impaired connectivity and cognitive impairment are group differences or within-cohort declines, not deficits against norms.

analysis.effect_sizes: All second-hand; no pooling. Dependence: about 9% of people who ever use (DSM-IV; ref 3, Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011); about 1 in 6 (17% in Table 1) of those who start as teenagers and 25–50% of people who smoke daily (ref 4, Hall & Degenhardt, 2009); people who start in adolescence about 2–4 times as likely as people who start as adults to have dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (ref 8, Chen et al., 2009); NSDUH 2012: 2.7 million people aged 12 or older with DSM-IV marijuana dependence, 5.1 million with dependence on any illicit drug and 8.6 million with alcohol dependence (ref 1). Psychosis: first episode brought forward by 2–6 years with heavier use, higher potency and younger exposure (ref 25, Di Forti et al., 2014). Driving: crash risk about 2 times when driving soon after use, attributed to a meta-analysis but cited to ref 37; drivers with THC in blood 3–7 times as likely to be culpable as drivers who had used neither drugs nor alcohol (ref 38); for comparison, crash risk almost 5 times at blood alcohol above 0.08% and 27 times for drivers younger than 21 (ref 39). Cancer: 30 or more joint-years associated with lung and upper aerodigestive cancers before, but not after, adjustment for confounders including tobacco (ref 40). Potency and services: THC in seized samples from about 3% (1980s) to 12% (2012) (ref 50); emergency department visits involving marijuana up 62% with other drugs and 100% alone from 2004 to 2011, P<0.05 (ref 51; Figure 1 legend). Table 2: high confidence for addiction to marijuana and other substances, diminished lifetime achievement, motor-vehicle accidents and symptoms of chronic bronchitis; medium for abnormal brain development, progression to use of other drugs, schizophrenia, and depression or anxiety; low for lung cancer.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level. The adjustment sets of the cited estimates are not given, except that the lung-cancer association is described before and after adjustment for confounders such as tobacco smoking; no estimate is described as adjusted for socioeconomic status, other drug use or premorbid functioning.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection of harms. Contrary or null findings appear in the body (deficits that may be reversible and subtle; shared environmental factors behind early use and school dropout; a lung-cancer association that disappeared after adjustment; no significant long-term effect of low exposure on lung function; a common-liability explanation of the gateway association) but not in the tables or the conclusions. The published critique of the Dunedin IQ finding (Rogeberg, 2013) and the reply (Moffitt et al., 2013), both in the journal that published that finding and both before this review, are not mentioned.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As cited, about 9% of people who ever use marijuana develop DSM-IV dependence, more among those who start young; regular use is associated with anxiety, depression and psychosis, with causality not established; cross-sectional imaging differences and one cohort's IQ decline are reported for use beginning in adolescence; recent use roughly doubles crash risk; regular smoking goes with symptoms of chronic bronchitis; the lung-cancer association did not survive adjustment. The body names confounding and shared predisposition as obstacles to causal inference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The tables present these associations as effects. Table 1 lists them as effects of short-term and of long-term or heavy use (for example cognitive impairment, with lower IQ among people who used frequently in adolescence), and Table 2 gives high confidence to addiction, diminished lifetime achievement, motor-vehicle accidents and bronchitis symptoms with no stated method, its footnote speaking of association while its title speaks of adverse effects. The body says the evidence suggests that such use "results in measurable and long-lasting cognitive impairments", on the strength of one cohort (Meier et al., 2012; ADVERSE EFFECTS › EFFECT ON SCHOOL PERFORMANCE AND LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT, 1st paragraph) and that long-term heavy use produces memory and attention impairments that worsen with years of use, citing a treatment-seeking sample (Solowij et al., 2002), in the same section that cites evidence that deficits may be reversible and subtle. It says long-term exposure impairs driving but cites nothing on long-term exposure. High confidence in diminished lifetime achievement sits beside the body's statement that shared environmental factors suggest a more complex relationship. Against this, the conclusions are hedged (repeated use in adolescence may cause long-lasting changes in brain function), and the limitations section concedes that confounding limits causal inference for most long-term effects.

timeline.event: Treatment-seeking sample with long-term heavy use (Solowij et al., 2002), cited as showing memory and attention deficits that persist and worsen with years of use.
Systematic review of longitudinal general-population studies of psychological and social sequelae (Macleod et al., 2004), cited for deficits that may be reversible and subtle after abstinence.

Dunedin study of COMT moderation of adolescent-onset use and adult psychosis (Caspi et al., 2005), cited for a link with psychosis strongest in people with a genetic vulnerability; Murray et al. (2016) describe attempted replications as inconsistent (card sc_murray_2016).
Population case–control study of lung and upper aerodigestive cancers (Hashibe et al., 2006): association with 30 or more joint-years not present after adjustment, as described here.

NESARC transition probabilities, the source of the review's 9%: 8.9% lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV cannabis dependence after first use; onset before 14 predicted transition before adjustment, but the direction reversed after adjustment (hazard ratio 0.63, 0.5 to 0.9), per card sc_lopez_quintero_2011.
Dunedin cohort IQ decline with persistent use (Meier et al., 2012), the review's only source for IQ decline.
CARDIA 20-year lung-function study, cited for no significant long-term effect of low exposure (card sc_pletcher_2012).

Meta-analysis of nine crash studies, pooled odds ratio 1.92 (1.35 to 2.73) for recent use (card sc_asbridge_2012); not cited directly, although the review gives a roughly doubled risk from a meta-analysis.

Published critique attributing the Dunedin IQ association to socioeconomic confounding (Rogeberg, 2013) and the Dunedin authors' reply (Moffitt et al., 2013); both appeared before this review and neither is mentioned.
Twin study asking whether the link between early-onset use and educational attainment is causal or due to common liability (Verweij et al., 2013), cited for shared environmental factors.

40-year Swedish conscript cohort on lung cancer, cited only as not ruling out a positive association; card sc_callaghan_2013 records a fully adjusted hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14) for more than 50 lifetime uses.
South London study of age at onset of psychosis by frequency and potency of use (Di Forti et al., 2014), cited for onset brought forward by 2–6 years.
After this review: re-analysis of the 2012 crash meta-analyses with lower corrected estimates (card sc_rogeberg_2016), relevant to the doubled crash risk given here.

After this review: two longitudinal twin studies of adolescent use and IQ (Jackson et al., 2016) and a co-twin control study (Meier et al., 2018), the within-family tests of the IQ association on which the review relies; both are read in this round.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely cited 2014 summary by NIDA authors. Its 9% dependence figure traces to US surveys, but its adolescent-onset and daily-use figures come through a secondary review, which does not contain the daily-use figure; its doubled crash risk predates the 2016 re-analysis that lowered the pooled estimates; its IQ claim rests on the Dunedin cohort, whose interpretation was disputed in 2013 and tested in twin studies from 2016. Cite it for the authors' 2014 judgments, labelled as theirs, and take numbers from the primary studies.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: The article states that no potential conflict of interest relevant to it was reported; the authors' disclosure forms are on NEJM.org and were not read (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are at the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, as printed. Several data sources cited are US federal surveys and surveillance systems (NSDUH and DAWN, refs 1 and 51). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For the review's central long-term claims: cohorts with cognitive testing before first use and repeated testing during use and after sustained abstinence, analysed within twin or sibling pairs with socioeconomic covariates; repeated population cohorts reporting the cumulative probability of DSM-5 cannabis use disorder by frequency, age of onset and measured THC exposure; and a systematic review grading each effect by a stated method, in place of the unexplained confidence ratings of Table 2.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the areas where they judged the evidence strongest.

No appraisal of individual studies, yet Table 2 grades confidence in each effect with no stated method or criteria; designs and sample sizes of cited studies are rarely given, cross-sectional imaging differences are called impaired connectivity, and several figures are attributed to secondary sources or to a source that does not contain them (reporting issues 1 and 2).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 77 references has one of the authors in its printed author list (editors' count).

Some speculation is labelled (assuming that the inverse relation between perceived risk and use is causal; a hypothesis that legalization will increase use and harm; potency that may account for more emergency visits), but other inferences are stated as findings or near-findings (students functioning below their capability for long periods; evidence said to suggest that heavy use results in lasting cognitive impairment, from one cohort).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against harm
domains.note: The body reports some null and contrary findings (reversible or subtle deficits, shared environmental factors, a null adjusted cancer association, no long-term effect of low lung exposure, a common-liability explanation of the gateway link), but the tables and conclusions leave them out and the 2013 critique of the IQ finding is not mentioned: the evidence against harm is under-represented where readers look first. Benefits are outside the scope by design.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment follows the worst domains. The review describes no search, and its confidence ratings, the part most often quoted, come with no method. Cite it for the authors' 2014 judgments (labelled as theirs, never as graded evidence) and as a pointer to the primary studies named in the key findings; take every number from the primary study, and do not use the 25–50% daily-use dependence figure, whose cited source does not contain it. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft and must say its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Scope: the review summarizes the adverse health effects of recreational marijuana use, focusing on the areas where the authors judge the evidence strongest; it notes that some studies have reported detrimental effects and others have not and that whether marijuana is harmful remains debated. No search, inclusion criteria or appraisal method is described; potential medical uses appear only in a box.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 2nd paragraph; LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE, 3rd paragraph and box

key_findings.finding: Use: about 12% of people aged 12 or older in the USA reported past-year use (ref 1, NSDUH); inhalation is named as the most common route, with oral use also mentioned. In the 2013 Monitoring the Future survey, 6.5% of grade-12 students reported daily or near-daily use, probably an underestimate because young people who have left school may use more often (refs 26, 27).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph; ADVERSE EFFECTS › EFFECT ON SCHOOL PERFORMANCE AND LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Dependence risk: about 9% of people who experiment with marijuana become dependent by DSM-IV criteria (ref 3, Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011), about 1 in 6 of those who start as teenagers and 25–50% of those who smoke daily (ref 4, Hall & Degenhardt, 2009); Table 1 gives 9% overall, 17% of those who begin in adolescence and 25–50% of people who use daily. The authors conclude that the evidence clearly shows that long-term use can lead to addiction.
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Second-hand. The 9% matches the 8.9% lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence after first use in NESARC (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011); other reviews take the same 9% from the 1990–92 National Comorbidity Survey (9.1%, DSM-III-R; card sc_anthony_1994). Hall & Degenhardt (2009) give one in six for adolescent onset, citing a book chapter (Anthony, 2006), but no dependence figure for daily use (searched in the project's text extraction of that review, p. 1386; card sc_hall_2009): the 25–50% has no traceable source here.

key_findings.finding: In the 2012 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, an estimated 2.7 million people aged 12 or older met DSM-IV criteria for marijuana dependence, against 5.1 million for dependence on any illicit drug and 8.6 million for alcohol (ref 1). A cannabis withdrawal syndrome (irritability, sleep difficulties, dysphoria, craving, anxiety) is described as recognized and as making cessation difficult and contributing to relapse (ref 5, by its title a paper on diagnostic criteria for the syndrome).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Age at first use: people who start in adolescence are about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start as adults to show dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (ref 8, Chen, Storr & Anthony, 2009); early and regular use predicts dependence, which in turn predicts use of other illicit drugs (ref 7). The authors attribute adolescent vulnerability probably to the active development of the brain, including the endocannabinoid system, in adolescence (ref 6).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: An unadjusted gradient as described. In NESARC, the source of the review's 9%, onset before 14 predicted transition to cannabis dependence before adjustment (hazard ratio 2.47), but the direction reversed after adjustment (0.63, 0.5 to 0.9), which that study's authors read as early onset marking psychiatric and substance comorbidity rather than causing dependence (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011).

key_findings.finding: Imaging, as cited: adults who smoked regularly in adolescence had fewer fibres (impaired connectivity) in the precuneus and the fimbria of the hippocampus than unexposed controls (ref 12, Zalesky et al., 2012); reduced functional connectivity in prefrontal inhibitory-control networks and in subcortical networks is reported (ref 13), and imaging studies show lower prefrontal activity and smaller hippocampal volumes (ref 14, a systematic review). Cortical CB1 receptor down-regulation in people who smoked long-term correlated with years of smoking and reversed after 4 weeks of abstinence, with no change in subcortical regions (ref 15, Hirvonen et al., 2012). Animal studies are cited for prenatal and adolescent THC effects on reward sensitivity and axonal development (refs 10, 11, 17).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › EFFECT ON BRAIN DEVELOPMENT, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Cross-sectional group differences; the review gives no sample sizes or effect sizes. The authors infer that some brain regions may be more vulnerable than others.

key_findings.finding: IQ: the authors say the effect of use on brain connectivity is most marked with onset in adolescence or young adulthood (ref 12), which may explain why frequent use from adolescence into adulthood was associated with a significant fall in IQ (ref 16, Meier et al., 2012); later they state that the evidence suggests long-term or heavy use causes measurable, lasting cognitive impairment, particularly with onset in early adolescence (ref 16).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › EFFECT ON BRAIN DEVELOPMENT, 3rd paragraph; ADVERSE EFFECTS › EFFECT ON SCHOOL PERFORMANCE AND LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: One cohort, no numbers given. In Meier et al. (2012) the decline was about 6 IQ points (−0.38 SD) in the 38 people with 3 or more waves of dependence and about 8 points in the 23 of them whose dependence began in adolescence (card sc_meier_2012). The 2013 critique (Rogeberg) and reply (Moffitt et al.) are not mentioned.

key_findings.finding: Because marijuana impairs critical cognitive functions during intoxication and for days after use (ref 28, a review), the authors infer that many students may spend long stretches working cognitively below their potential, and that failure to learn while intoxicated may also explain the association between regular use and poor grades (ref 29).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › EFFECT ON SCHOOL PERFORMANCE AND LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The inference about students' functioning is the authors' own; no study of functioning at school is cited.

key_findings.finding: Conflicting cognitive and psychosocial evidence, as cited: one strand suggests that deficits after long-term use may reverse with abstinence and stay subtle rather than disabling (ref 30, Macleod et al., 2004); others that long-term heavy use results in memory and attention impairments that persist and worsen with years of regular use (ref 31, Solowij et al., 2002) and with initiation in adolescence (ref 32). Early use is associated with poorer school performance and a higher risk of dropping out (refs 27, 29), but shared environmental factors influencing both early use and dropout (ref 33, Verweij et al., 2013) suggest a more complex relationship. Heavy use has been linked to lower income, more need for socioeconomic assistance, unemployment, criminal behaviour and lower life satisfaction (refs 2, 34).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › EFFECT ON SCHOOL PERFORMANCE AND LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mental illness: regular use is linked to a higher risk of anxiety and depression, without established causality (ref 23, Patton et al., 2002). Marijuana is linked with psychoses, including those of schizophrenia, especially in people with a pre-existing genetic vulnerability (ref 24, Caspi et al., 2005, a COMT gene–environment study), and is said to worsen the course of illness in schizophrenia (no citation); heavier use, greater potency and younger exposure can bring forward the first psychotic episode by 2 to 6 years (ref 25, Di Forti et al., 2014). The authors add that factors other than marijuana, and factors that predispose to both use and mental illness, make it difficult to attribute the increased risk to marijuana.
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RELATION TO MENTAL ILLNESS, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No estimate of the size of the psychosis risk is given. The genetic-vulnerability statement rests on one candidate-gene study whose attempted replications Murray et al. (2016) describe as inconsistent (card sc_murray_2016); Moore et al. (2007) called the evidence for COMT effect modification very weak (card sc_moore_2007).

key_findings.finding: Gateway: rodent studies show that adolescent cannabinoid exposure reduces the reactivity of dopamine neurons that modulate reward regions (ref 18), prenatal exposure alters mesolimbic dopamine development (ref 19) and THC primes responses to other drugs (ref 21); most epidemiological studies report greater later susceptibility to other drugs (ref 20). The authors note that alcohol and nicotine also prime the brain (ref 22) and give an alternative explanation without a citation: people more susceptible to drug use may start with marijuana because it is accessible, and their contacts with others who use drugs raise the chance of trying other drugs.
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › POSSIBLE ROLE AS GATEWAY DRUG, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Driving: immediate and long-term exposure are both said to impair driving; marijuana is the illicit drug most often reported in impaired driving and crashes, including fatal ones (ref 35). Blood THC relates to performance in driving-simulator studies (ref 36); recent smoking and blood THC of 2–5 ng/mL are associated with substantial impairment, and the risk of crash involvement roughly doubles when a person drives soon after use, according to a meta-analysis (both cited to ref 37). In a culpability analysis, drivers with THC in blood (typical detection minimum 1 ng/mL), especially at higher levels, were 3 to 7 times more likely to be culpable for a crash than drivers who had used neither drugs nor alcohol (ref 38). For comparison, crash risk rises almost 5 times at blood alcohol above 0.08% and 27 times for drivers younger than 21, the sentence not saying at what alcohol level (ref 39); alcohol combined with marijuana appears riskier than either alone (ref 37).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF MOTOR-VEHICLE ACCIDENTS, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand, and the figures come from different designs (crash involvement, culpability, alcohol crash risk) that are not directly comparable. The meta-analysis behind the doubled risk is not named (reporting issue 2); the 2012 meta-analysis of Asbridge et al. pooled 1.92 (1.35 to 2.73), later lowered on re-analysis (cards sc_asbridge_2012, sc_rogeberg_2016). No study of long-term exposure and driving is cited.

key_findings.finding: Lung cancer: smoking the equivalent of 30 or more joint-years (one joint a day for a year) was associated with more lung and upper aerodigestive cancers, but the association disappeared after adjustment for confounders such as tobacco smoking (ref 40, Hashibe et al., 2006); a positive association cannot be ruled out (ref 41, Callaghan et al., 2013), but the evidence suggests the risk is lower than with tobacco (ref 40); smoking marijuana mixed with tobacco is a confounder whose prevalence varies greatly between countries. The authors call the effect on lung cancer unclear, and Table 2 gives it low confidence.
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF CANCER AND OTHER EFFECTS ON HEALTH, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Callaghan et al. (2013) reported a fully adjusted hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14) for more than 50 lifetime uses in Swedish conscripts (card sc_callaghan_2013); the review's wording (a positive association cannot be ruled out) understates that result.

key_findings.finding: Other effects on health: marijuana smoking is associated with inflammation of the large airways, higher airway resistance and lung hyperinflation, and people who smoke regularly report more symptoms of chronic bronchitis than people who do not smoke (ref 42, Tashkin, 2013), while low levels of exposure do not appear to have a significant long-term effect (ref 43, Pletcher et al., 2012); respiratory infections and pneumonia are more frequent (ref 44). Use has been associated with vascular conditions that raise the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication (ref 45, a review); direct effects on CB1 receptors in arterial vessels and indirect effects on vasoactive compounds may explain effects on vascular resistance and coronary microcirculation (refs 46, 47).
key_findings.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF CANCER AND OTHER EFFECTS ON HEALTH, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Ref 47 is, by its title, a report of coronary no-flow and ventricular tachycardia with habitual marijuana use, so the coronary-microcirculation statement rests on a case report and a review.

key_findings.finding: Limitations and potency: most long-term effects summarized were seen in people who used heavily or for long periods, and multiple, often hidden, confounders (including use with other drugs) limit causal attribution; understanding of prenatal exposure in humans is very poor (refs 48, 49). THC content of seized samples rose steadily from about 3% in the 1980s to 12% in 2012 (ref 50); the authors say this raises concern that consequences may be worse now, may account for the significant rise in emergency department visits by people reporting marijuana use (ref 51) and in fatal crashes (ref 35), and questions the relevance of older long-term studies. Figure 1 legend: of marijuana, cocaine and heroin, only marijuana showed significant increases in emergency visits from 2004 to 2011, 62% in combination with other drugs and 100% alone (P<0.05 for both).
key_findings.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Figure 1 legend
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image; values were not extracted beyond the legend, whose potency panel covers 1995–2012, so the 1980s value is not shown in it. The link from potency to emergency visits and crashes is ecological and offered as a possibility.

key_findings.finding: Vomiting: in the box on medical uses, THC is called an effective antiemetic in chemotherapy (ref 59) and patients are said often to find marijuana more effective; repeated use has, paradoxically, been linked to increased vomiting (hyperemesis), a statement given without a citation.
key_findings.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE › box (Clinical Conditions with Symptoms That May Be Relieved by Treatment with Marijuana or Other Cannabinoids) › Nausea
key_findings.note: The statement that patients often find marijuana more effective than THC carries no citation; ref 59 (Sallan et al., 1975) sits on the preceding clause.

key_findings.finding: Medical uses: the 1999 Institute of Medicine report is cited for potential benefits for appetite in AIDS-related wasting, chemotherapy-related nausea and vomiting, severe pain and some spasticity, and some evidence on intraocular pressure in glaucoma (ref 52); the authors say some physicians continue to prescribe marijuana despite limited evidence of benefit. The box cites, among others, no rigorous evidence of a sustained benefit in AIDS-related morbidity and mortality (ref 62), nabiximols in multiple sclerosis (refs 70, 71), and a parent survey of CBD-rich cannabis in childhood epilepsy in which 2 of 19 families (11%) reported freedom from seizures, 8 (42%) a reduction of more than 80% and 6 (32%) a reduction of 25–60% (ref 72), with insufficient safety and efficacy data (ref 73). Marijuana may worsen HIV-associated cognitive deficits (ref 75).
key_findings.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE, 3rd paragraph and box (Glaucoma; AIDS-associated anorexia and wasting syndrome; Multiple sclerosis; Epilepsy)

key_findings.finding: Policy and perceived risk: among adolescents, use has been inversely correlated with perceived risk (Figure 2A); assuming that this relation is causal, the authors ask whether greater permissiveness would expose more young people to regular use; the reported prevalence of regular smoking among grade-12 students has been rising and may soon cross the trend line for regular tobacco smoking (Figure 2B; ref 26). The effects of second-hand exposure to marijuana smoke are not clearly understood (ref 76).
key_findings.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE, 4th paragraph; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: Figure 2 is an image; its values were not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Table 1. Short-term use: impaired short-term memory, impaired motor coordination (driving, injuries), altered judgment (sexual risk behaviour), and paranoia and psychosis at high doses. Long-term or heavy use: addiction (9%, 17% and 25–50%, as above), altered brain development, poor educational outcome with more school dropout, cognitive impairment with lower IQ among people who used frequently in adolescence, diminished life satisfaction and achievement, symptoms of chronic bronchitis, and increased risk of chronic psychotic disorders including schizophrenia in people predisposed to them. The footnote marks five of these (addiction, brain development, education, cognition, life satisfaction) as strongly associated with use beginning early in adolescence.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and its footnote

key_findings.finding: Table 2, overall level of confidence: high for addiction to marijuana and other substances, diminished lifetime achievement, motor-vehicle accidents and symptoms of chronic bronchitis; medium for abnormal brain development, progression to use of other drugs, schizophrenia, and depression or anxiety; low for lung cancer. The footnote calls the ratings "an attempt to rank the strength of the current evidence" for an association, especially for heavy or long-term use and use beginning in adolescence; no method or criteria are given.
key_findings.locator: CONCLUSIONS › Table 2 and its footnote

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: marijuana use has been linked to substantial adverse effects, some of them established with high confidence in the authors' view; like other drugs, marijuana can result in addiction; intoxication interferes with cognitive and motor function, with consequences such as crashes; repeated use in adolescence may cause long-lasting changes in brain function that can threaten achievement in education, work and social life. Alcohol and tobacco account for the greatest drug-related burden of disease because their legal status allows wider exposure (ref 77), and the authors hypothesize that legalization will increase use and the number of people with negative health consequences.
key_findings.locator: CONCLUSIONS, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The figure of 25–50% dependence among people who smoke daily is cited to Hall & Degenhardt (2009, ref 4), whose dependence paragraph gives about 9% and one in six for adolescent onset but no figure for daily use (searched for daily, half, third and 25–50 in the project's text extraction of that review; p. 1386; card sc_hall_2009). Table 1 repeats the 25–50%.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The daily-use figure has no traceable source in this review and should not be cited from it. Estimates by frequency of use are in the primary surveys and in Leung et al. (2020): dependence in 33% (22 to 44) of people using weekly or daily in cohort studies and 18% (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies (card sc_leung_2020).

reporting_issues.issue: The roughly doubled crash risk is attributed to a meta-analysis but cited to ref 37, Hartman & Huestis (2013), whose title ("Cannabis effects on driving skills") does not describe a meta-analysis; the meta-analysis itself is not named.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF MOTOR-VEHICLE ACCIDENTS, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimate cannot be traced through this review; claims should cite the crash meta-analyses and their re-analysis directly (cards sc_asbridge_2012, sc_rogeberg_2016).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives confidence levels without any method or criteria; its title refers to adverse effects while its footnote refers to the association between use and each effect. It rates addiction to marijuana and other substances as high but progression to use of other drugs as medium, and lists schizophrenia without the restriction to predisposed people that Table 1 applies.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), CONCLUSIONS › Table 2; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The ratings are the authors' unexplained judgments and cannot be mapped to GRADE; they may be cited only as the authors' opinion, and not as high confidence for addiction to other substances.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements carry no citation or a citation that does not match them: that marijuana worsens the course of schizophrenia (no citation); the common-liability explanation of the gateway association (no citation); that driving-simulator studies predict real-world driving (ref 36 is a simulator study); that long-term exposure impairs driving (ref 35 concerns, by its title, trends in drugs detected in fatally injured drivers); and the report of hyperemesis with repeated use (no citation). In the box on medical uses, by the references' titles: ref 60, a study in the house musk shrew, is cited for other plant compounds enhancing THC's effect against nausea (an animal finding given without saying so); ref 74, a study of cannabidivarin-rich extracts in mice and rats, for cannabidiol's role as an antiepileptic in animal models; refs 55 and 56 (endocannabinoids in human eye tissue; the synthetic agonist WIN55212-2) for THC, cannabinol and nabilone, but not cannabidiol, lowering intraocular pressure in rabbits; and ref 58, a review of cannabidiol, for THC's early use against chemotherapy nausea. The statement that patients often find marijuana more effective than THC carries no citation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), ADVERSE EFFECTS › RELATION TO MENTAL ILLNESS, 1st paragraph; POSSIBLE ROLE AS GATEWAY DRUG, 1st paragraph; RISK OF MOTOR-VEHICLE ACCIDENTS, 1st paragraph; box › Nausea
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements cannot be anchored to evidence through this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 16 (Meier et al., 2012) is printed with the page range E2657–E2564, which ends before it starts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor typographical error; identify the paper by the DOI printed with the reference (10.1073/pnas.1206820109).
